hero.headline: FCC approves test satellite to beam sunlight from space despite astronomers' concerns
hero.body:
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Reflect Orbital to launch its first demonstration satellite, an 18-metre space mirror designed to reflect sunlight back to Earth during nighttime hours. The approval covers radio operations for the initial test satellite, part of a broader proposal that could eventually involve up to 50,000 satellites in low Earth orbit.

Reflect Orbital plans to position reflective surfaces in orbit that can redirect sunlight to specific locations on the ground, potentially providing illumination on demand. The company has positioned the technology as a way to extend daylight hours for various applications, though specific use cases have not been detailed in the approval documentation.

The authorization has drawn significant opposition from astronomers and space observation groups who warn that large-scale deployment of reflective satellites could interfere with astronomical observations and contribute to light pollution in the night sky. Critics argue that even a small number of highly reflective objects in orbit could create visible streaks across telescope images and disrupt scientific research that depends on dark skies.

The approved demonstration represents a single 18-metre mirror, far smaller in scale than the proposed constellation of 50,000 satellites that Reflect Orbital has outlined in its long-term plans. The FCC's approval focuses specifically on the radio frequency operations needed to control and communicate with the satellite, rather than addressing broader environmental or astronomical concerns.

The growing commercialization of low Earth orbit has raised questions about regulatory oversight of space-based activities that could affect ground conditions. While satellite constellations for communications have become routine, projects designed to actively manipulate light or other environmental factors from orbit represent a newer category of space activity. The test satellite will provide data on the technical feasibility of the concept and may inform future regulatory decisions about larger-scale deployments.

cards.headline: U.S. Gives Iran Deadline to Renounce Attacks on Ships in Strait of Hormuz
cards.body:
The United States has set a Saturday deadline for Iran to publicly renounce attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, according to multiple reports. Vice President JD Vance is expected to participate in negotiations resuming in Oman, where American and Iranian officials are working to de-escalate tensions over the strategic waterway.

The U.S. is seeking an Iranian pledge to stop shooting at ships traveling through the strait, a narrow passage that serves as a critical chokepoint for global oil shipments. Roughly one-fifth of the world's petroleum passes through this waterway, making it essential to international energy markets. Any disruption to shipping in the area could trigger widespread economic consequences and increase transportation costs worldwide.

The talks represent a diplomatic effort to resolve the maritime confrontation between the two nations. American officials have been working to secure commitments from Tehran that would guarantee safe passage for both commercial and military vessels through the waterway.

The negotiations come after a period of heightened tensions involving Iranian attacks on ships in the region. A memorandum of understanding signed between Iran and the U.S. last week included an agreement by Tehran to make its best efforts to ensure full freedom of navigation and to impose no fees or tolls for a minimum of 60 days.

However, complications have emerged in coordinating safe passage for vessels. The UN's International Maritime Organization proposed two temporary shipping evacuation lanes in conjunction with Oman. One route would run through mined Iranian waters to the north, while another would pass through more passable Omani waters to the south. The proposal aimed to help evacuate hundreds of ships that have been trapped in the area for months.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps rejected the proposed coordinates, calling alternative transit routes "unacceptable and completely dangerous." The statement emphasized that coordination with the IRGC navy would be mandatory for any transit through the strait. Iran has used control of the waterway as a negotiating lever in broader discussions about U.S. sanctions, asset relief, and its nuclear program.

Mohammad Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran's parliament and chief negotiator, stated that the administration of the strait would not return to conditions prior to February 28. "Everyone should know that the administration of the strait of Hormuz will never go back to the way it was before the war," he said.

Iran and Oman have agreed to establish a working party to discuss the future administration of the strait. Oman is pushing for any arrangement to comply with international maritime law, while the U.S. and other nations have warned against imposing fees or tolls that would violate fundamental principles of ocean navigation.

The outcome of the Saturday negotiations could determine whether the standoff escalates further or moves toward resolution.

cards.headline: Intelligence reports suggest Iran plans to target Trump
cards.teaser: Israel has shared intelligence with the United States indicating Iran intends to assassinate President Trump as the ceasefire between the two nations deteriorates.
cards.body:
Intelligence shared by Israel with the U.S. indicates Iran is planning to assassinate President Trump, according to reports this week. The reported threat highlights tensions between Washington and Tehran as a ceasefire between the two countries has broken down.

Vice President JD Vance and other U.S. officials are expected to participate in negotiations resuming Saturday in Oman, where discussions will include Iran's activities in the Strait of Hormuz.

cards.headline: Israel Defends Strike on Iranian Steel Facility as Military Target
cards.teaser: Israel struck Iranian steel plants during the war, claiming they provided revenue and weapons materials, though the attacks also damaged the civilian economy.
cards.body:
Israel attacked Iran's steel plants during recent hostilities, citing them as legitimate military targets. Israeli officials argued the facilities generated revenue for Iranian forces and supplied materials needed to manufacture weapons.

The strikes had broader economic consequences, damaging Iran's civilian steel industry, which supports commercial manufacturing and employment. The operation raised questions about the boundaries between military and civilian infrastructure during armed conflict.

cards.headline: American Aid Worker Tests Positive for Ebola in Democratic Republic of Congo
cards.teaser: A U.S. citizen working for a humanitarian organization in Congo has tested positive for Ebola, the CDC confirms.
cards.body:
An American aid worker has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The individual works for a humanitarian organization in the country.

The case emerges as Ebola continues spreading in Congo, with the death toll reaching 600. Authorities have reported new suspected cases in previously unaffected areas beyond the outbreak's epicenter in Ituri province, indicating the disease's continued expansion across the region.

cards.headline: Trump Administration Subpoenas New York Times Journalists Over Air Force One Reporting
cards.teaser: Multiple journalists at The New York Times received subpoenas following their reporting on security concerns surrounding the new Air Force One.
cards.body:
The Trump administration issued subpoenas to several New York Times journalists after the publication reported on security concerns related to the new Air Force One aircraft. The subpoenas represent an escalation in pressure on media organizations covering the administration.

The reporting in question focused on security issues surrounding the aircraft. The subpoenas mark a direct legal action against journalists for their coverage of government operations and security matters.

cards.headline: Trump fires two Democratic election commissioners ahead of midterms
cards.body:
President Trump has dismantled the U.S. Election Assistance Commission by removing all remaining members of the independent federal agency devoted to election administration, drawing accusations that he is attempting to manipulate the upcoming midterm elections.

Trump fired the two Democratic commissioners, Thomas Hicks and Benjamin Hovland, by email on Thursday, effective immediately. The sole remaining Republican commissioner, Christy McCormick, was pushed to resign rather than fired outright. A fourth seat had already been vacant since Republican Donald Palmer departed for the Heritage Foundation earlier this year. With no commissioners remaining, the agency cannot vote to take any formal action.

The White House justified the removals by citing the president's authority to remove officials and referenced a recent Supreme Court ruling that expanded his power to fire heads of independent agencies. However, election law scholars say the ruling's application to bipartisan bodies like the EAC remains untested, since Congress deliberately structured the commission around an equal partisan split.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the dismissals a "brazen attempt" to seize control of elections. "Firing every remaining member of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission months before the midterms is a brazen attempt to seize control of our elections before a single vote is cast," Schumer wrote on social media. He noted that the agency certifies voting systems and helps election officials run secure elections.

Derrick Johnson, president of the NAACP, accused Trump of rigging the election because he fears voters will reject his policies. "Donald Trump knows that in November voters will reject everything he stands for," Johnson said, pledging that the organization would work to send people to the polls.

The Election Assistance Commission distributes federal election security grants, maintains the national mail voter registration form, certifies voting machines against federal standards, and advises state and local officials. Created following the disputed 2000 election, it does not run elections itself but serves as a resource for cash-strapped states.

With the commission paralyzed, it cannot update voting standards or the federal registration form. This potentially freezes changes the administration has pushed for, including a citizenship documentation requirement that courts have already partially blocked.

Benjamin Hovland, one of the fired commissioners, warned that losing the agency risked administrative mistakes during the midterms. Democratic secretaries of state criticized the firings as irresponsible. Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar said the EAC plays a critical role supporting state and local election officials, and the dismissals would make it harder for election administrators to do their work.

Replacements would require Senate confirmation, a process that could extend well past the midterm elections.

cards.headline: Spain Battles Deadly Wildfire as Death Toll Reaches at Least 12
cards.teaser: Spanish authorities work to contain one of the country's deadliest wildfires, with at least four British nationals believed among the victims.
cards.body:
A major wildfire in southeastern Spain's Almería province has killed at least 12 people, with 23 others still missing. Four of the victims are believed to be British nationals. The blaze struck the area near the village of Bédar in Los Gallardos municipality, with many deaths occurring as people attempted to flee the flames.

The disaster comes as Spain endures its second heatwave of the summer. Authorities in the Andalucía region are working to contain the fast-spreading fire, which ranks among the deadliest wildfires in recent Spanish history.

cards.headline: American Aid Worker Tests Positive for Ebola in Democratic Republic of Congo
cards.teaser: A U.S. citizen working for a humanitarian organization in Congo has tested positive for Ebola, the CDC confirms.
cards.body:
An American aid worker has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The individual works for a humanitarian organization in the country.

The case emerges as Ebola continues spreading in Congo, with the death toll reaching 600. Authorities have reported new suspected cases in previously unaffected areas beyond the outbreak's epicenter in Ituri province, indicating the disease's continued expansion across the region.

cards.headline: Man Arrested in Killing of Former U.K. Lawmaker Ann Widdecombe Released
cards.teaser: British police release a 26-year-old man who had been arrested in connection with the death of former MP Ann Widdecombe.
cards.body:
Police in the United Kingdom have released a 26-year-old man arrested in connection with the death of Ann Widdecombe, a former member of Parliament. The man is no longer considered part of the investigation.

Widdecombe served in Parliament and remained a prominent public figure after leaving office. Police continue investigating her death and have asked anyone with information about the crime to contact them.

cards.headline: Canada-U.S. Border Bridge Set to Open After Trump Administration Delays
cards.teaser: A new bridge linking Canada and the United States will open after a deal ended the Trump administration's blocking of the project.
cards.body:
A new bridge connecting Canada and the United States is set to open following an agreement that resolved delays imposed during the Trump administration. The bridge is designed to ease congestion at the busiest trade corridor between the two countries.

The project had been blocked by the previous administration but moved forward after negotiations produced a deal acceptable to both nations. The crossing is expected to improve the flow of commercial traffic and reduce wait times at one of North America's most heavily used border points.

cards.headline: New Dinosaur Species Discovered in Thailand Measured as Long as Cricket Pitch
cards.teaser: Scientists have identified a plant-eating dinosaur in Thailand that lived approximately 150 million years ago.
cards.body:
Researchers in Thailand have identified a previously unknown dinosaur species, which they named Uragasaurus kalasinensis. This herbivorous dinosaur roamed the Earth approximately 150 million years ago during the Jurassic period and reached lengths comparable to a cricket pitch.

The fossil discovery enhances scientific knowledge about the variety of dinosaur species that inhabited Southeast Asia millions of years ago.

hero.headline: Flash Flooding in Missouri Prompts State of Emergency, Over 100 Rescued
hero.body:
Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe declared a state of emergency Friday after severe storms unleashed intense flash flooding across central, south-central, and southeastern regions of the state. The declaration activates Missouri's state emergency operations plan, enabling state agencies to coordinate directly with local jurisdictions and expedite emergency assistance.

"Over the past 24 hours, intense storms have created dangerous flash flooding across several regions of Missouri, resulting in multiple swift-water rescues," Kehoe said in a statement. "Activating the plan allows our agencies to move quickly, coordinate resources, and support local response efforts."

The flash flooding triggered extensive rescue operations across multiple counties. Flash flood warnings were in effect for parts of Iron, Reynolds, Andrew, Madison, Washington, Buchanan, Crawford, Clinton, DeKalb, and Holt counties. The U.S. National Weather Service issued a Flash Flood Emergency specifically for parts of Iron and Reynolds counties on Friday.

Some areas received between 6 and 12 inches of rain from Thursday night into Friday morning, creating what the National Weather Service described as "extensive and catastrophic flash flooding across eastern Missouri." The heavy rainfall fell on already saturated soil, significantly increasing flood risk and the intensity of the flooding.

A state task force with 50 trained members, specialized equipment, and rescue boats was deployed to affected areas. The Missouri state highway patrol, state emergency management agency, division of fire safety, Missouri state parks, and the Missouri department of conservation coordinated with local emergency responders to assist communities impacted by flooding that affected homes, roads, and campgrounds.

The flooding threat extended beyond Friday. The National Weather Service warned that additional rounds of thunderstorms with heavy rainfall were expected to continue through Friday evening, with a flood watch remaining in effect over the weekend. The Kansas City office of the National Weather Service cautioned that damaging winds and heavy rainfall posed primary threats, though hail and brief tornadoes could not be ruled out.

"Storms will be efficient producers of torrential rainfall that could lead to flooding," forecasters noted.

Governor Kehoe cautioned that "the threat is not over" and warned of additional heavy rain expected through the weekend. He urged residents in affected areas to stay alert and avoid driving or walking through flooded roads.

"If you're camping, floating, or spending time near rivers and streams, move to higher ground and stay alert of weather conditions," Kehoe advised. "Missourians should continue to monitor local forecasts and follow the guidance of local authorities."

Rescue operations remained ongoing Friday as authorities worked to account for all residents and visitors in flood-affected areas while assessing the full extent of damage to homes, businesses, and infrastructure.

cards.headline: Trump Administration Subpoenas New York Times Journalists Over Air Force One Reporting
cards.teaser: Multiple journalists at The New York Times received subpoenas following their reporting on security concerns surrounding the new Air Force One.
cards.body:
The Trump administration issued subpoenas to several New York Times journalists after the publication reported on security concerns related to the new Air Force One aircraft. The subpoenas represent an escalation in pressure on media organizations covering the administration.

The reporting in question focused on security issues surrounding the aircraft. The subpoenas mark a direct legal action against journalists for their coverage of government operations and security matters.

cards.headline: Minnesota Withdraws National Guard from Washington Early
cards.teaser: Governor Tim Walz is pulling Minnesota National Guard troops from Washington ahead of schedule as criticism mounts over Democratic governors sending forces to the capital.
cards.body:
Minnesota Governor Tim Walz announced he is withdrawing his state's National Guard troops from Washington, D.C. ahead of schedule. The decision reflects mounting opposition among Democratic governors to maintaining troop deployments in the capital while President Trump continues his own military presence there.

The move puts pressure on other Democratic governors who sent National Guard units to Washington. Michigan has drawn particular attention, with growing calls for the state to recall its troops from the capital as well.

cards.headline: Burmese Pythons Establish New Population Center in Florida
cards.teaser: Wildlife experts say invasive Burmese pythons have established a new hot spot in Florida as the species continues expanding its range.
cards.body:
Invasive Burmese pythons have established a new concentration area in Florida, according to wildlife experts tracking the species' spread. Florida crews recently found two 17-foot pythons together, likely hunting white-tailed deer in the region.

The state has deployed hunters to the Everglades to control the python population, with one participant potentially earning up to $10,000. Wildlife officials warn hunters never to cut off the heads of captured pythons due to safety concerns. Maps tracking the species show continued expansion beyond their traditional range in South Florida.

cards.headline: White Nationalist Group Patriot Front Marches in Washington on July Fourth
cards.teaser: Hundreds of masked members of the white nationalist group Patriot Front marched in Washington on Independence Day.
cards.body:
Hundreds of masked members of the white nationalist group Patriot Front marched through Washington on July Fourth. The demonstrators wore uniforms and face coverings during the event in the nation's capital.

The march marked one of the larger gatherings of white nationalist groups in Washington in recent years. The group's membership composition and funding sources remain subjects of public inquiry.

cards.headline: Virtual Reality Dance Apps Offer Judgment-Free Learning Experience
cards.teaser: New virtual reality applications aim to help people learn partner dancing without the social pressure of traditional dance floors.
cards.body:
Virtual reality dance apps like Dance Guru and Trip the Light help people learn partner dancing in private settings. These applications use virtual partners to guide users through dance steps and techniques without an audience.

The apps appeal to people who feel shy or self-conscious about dancing in front of others. By providing a judgment-free environment, they allow learners to build confidence and practice fundamental skills before attempting partner dancing in real-world social situations.

cards.headline: Spain Faces Deadly Wildfire with 12 Killed, 23 Missing
cards.teaser: Spanish authorities are working to contain one of the country's deadliest wildfires, which has killed at least 12 people including four believed to be British nationals.
cards.body:
A devastating wildfire in Spain's southern province of Almeria has killed at least 12 people and left 23 others missing. The blaze ranks among Spain's deadliest wildfires in recent years. At least four British nationals are believed to be among the victims.

Emergency crews continue working to contain the flames and search for missing individuals. Several victims were discovered inside burnt-out vehicles, having died while attempting to flee the advancing fire in this popular holiday destination.

hero.headline: Apple Sues OpenAI for Trade Secret Theft
hero.body:
Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Friday, alleging that the artificial intelligence company stole trade secrets to advance its hardware business plans. The suit claims OpenAI recruited Apple employees and persuaded them to share confidential material, product designs, and proprietary information.

"Recently, significant evidence has emerged suggesting individuals employed by OpenAI wrongfully took Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products," Apple said in a statement. OpenAI's spokesperson said the company was reviewing the filing and denied the allegations. "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets. We remain focused on building innovative technology that empowers people everywhere," the spokesperson stated.

The lawsuit represents a dramatic reversal for the two companies, which announced a major partnership in 2024 to integrate OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot into Apple's operating systems. However, when Apple recently unveiled its redesigned Siri voice assistant, it used Google's Gemini AI model rather than ChatGPT.

The tension between the companies intensified last year when OpenAI spent 6.4 billion dollars to acquire io Products, a hardware startup founded by Jony Ive, a legendary Apple design executive. Apple's complaint names both OpenAI and io Products as defendants.

"OpenAI's nascent hardware business now rests on the shakiest of foundations, rotten to its core by its illegal reliance on misappropriated trade secrets," Apple wrote in its complaint.

The suit names specific former Apple employees now working at OpenAI. Tang Yew Tan, who serves as OpenAI's chief hardware officer and previously worked as a vice-president at Apple, allegedly directed job candidates still employed at Apple to bring "actual parts" from Apple to interviews for "show and tell" sessions. This conduct allowed Tan and his team to obtain additional confidential information, according to the complaint.

Another former Apple employee, Chang Liu, is accused of taking an Apple laptop when he left the company and using an authentication vulnerability to breach Apple's internal network. Liu allegedly downloaded dozens of confidential files related to Apple's hardware development.

The complaint alleges that this misconduct was directed by OpenAI's senior leadership and targeted trade secrets across multiple levels of Apple's organization. Apple is seeking damages and a court order preventing OpenAI from possessing or using its stolen trade secrets.

"Our teams are constantly developing breakthrough technologies to create the best products and services in the world, and protecting their work and intellectual property is something we take very seriously," an Apple spokesperson said. The case highlights growing tensions over intellectual property protection as technology companies compete intensely for engineering talent and race to develop new artificial intelligence hardware.

cards.headline: Micron Announces $250 Billion Investment in AI Chip Manufacturing
cards.teaser: The semiconductor company announced a major expansion for artificial intelligence memory chip development.
cards.body:
Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra announced a $250 billion investment to expand memory chip production for artificial intelligence. The company's Central New York facility reached a construction milestone with its first concrete pour in the Town of Clay, representing one of the largest private investments in the state's history.

The announcement reflects the global demand surge for advanced memory chips as companies race to build AI datacenters. President Trump attended the celebration, while Governor Kathy Hochul marked the progress on the semiconductor manufacturing site.

cards.headline: Oregon Drops Motion to Delay Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
cards.teaser: The state withdrew its attempt to block the media merger after other states declined to join the challenge.
cards.body:
Oregon's attorney general withdrew a motion seeking to delay the merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. The state also dropped its demand for records related to the transaction, which has been approved by the Trump administration.

Oregon was the only state attempting to pause the acquisition. Other states that had been considering legal action to block the deal did not file suits by expected deadlines. The merger represents a major consolidation in the media and entertainment industry.

cards.headline: Housing Bill Signed Into Law With Incentives for Local Builders
cards.teaser: The new legislation offers local governments and builders incentives to increase housing construction.
cards.body:
The 21st Century Road to Housing Act became law without President Trump's signature, automatically passing after Congress approved it with large bipartisan margins. The president declined to sign the legislation, citing concerns over voting restrictions, but his refusal to veto allowed it to proceed.

The measure represents the biggest change to federal housing policy in decades. It provides incentives for local governments and builders to increase housing availability through incremental changes and encourages construction and development across different communities.

cards.headline: Slate Auto Unveils $25,000 Electric Pickup Truck
cards.teaser: The company is entering the electric vehicle market with an affordable, no-frills pickup truck.
cards.body:
Slate Auto introduced an electric pickup truck priced at $25,000, drawing attention for its relatively affordable price point and stripped-down approach. The vehicle eliminates many features found in more expensive electric trucks in favor of basic functionality.

The company is entering a challenging market for electric vehicles, where several manufacturers have struggled with production costs and consumer demand. The low price represents a different strategy from premium-priced electric trucks that have dominated early market offerings.

cards.headline: Trump Accounts Prompt Parents to Invest for Children's Futures
cards.teaser: New investment accounts and child-friendly platforms have made it easier for parents to save for their children.
cards.body:
The White House has promoted Trump accounts as a way to give new generations a stake in the American dream. These accounts are part of a broader range of child-focused investment platforms that make it easier for parents to save for their children's future needs, including education and housing.

The initiative has generated both support and criticism. As with other long-term savings programs designed for younger beneficiaries, Trump accounts represent an expansion in options available to families looking to build wealth for the next generation.

cards.headline: Record Number of Young Adults Living With Parents
cards.teaser: Housing costs and economic conditions have pushed nearly half of young adults to live at home.
cards.body:
A record 49 percent of young adults now live with their parents, an increase of 12 percentage points since 2019. Economists say the pandemic and its economic aftermath contributed to the shift, with housing affordability playing a major role.

Age during the pandemic appears to correlate with current homeownership rates, according to research. Analysts say the trend could reshape patterns around marriage, having children, and home buying for an entire generation. Some economists note that living at home has shifted from a sign of failure to a financially prudent choice given current economic conditions.

cards.headline: Meta removes Instagram AI feature following user criticism
cards.teaser: The company pulled a creative tool that allowed AI systems to reference public user content after widespread negative feedback.
cards.body:
Meta has disabled an Instagram feature that allowed users to generate AI images based on content from public accounts by simply tagging them. The feature would have let anyone use a public account's posts as reference material for AI creations without the account owner's permission.

The company announced the decision in a blog post acknowledging user feedback. Meta said it had intended to provide a creative tool while giving people control over their content, but acknowledged the implementation missed the mark.

cards.headline: Shopping app Phia accused of taking unearned affiliate commissions
cards.teaser: The startup founded by Phoebe Gates allegedly used cookie stuffing to claim credit for purchases it did not generate.
cards.body:
Phia, a shopping app founded by Phoebe Gates and Sophia Kianni, is facing accusations of "cookie stuffing," according to a Bloomberg investigation. The practice involves placing tracking cookies on user devices to claim affiliate commissions for purchases the app did not actually drive.

Through cookie stuffing, Phia received commissions and credit for sales it did not legitimately generate. This affiliate marketing scheme allows companies to fraudulently collect fees that are typically reserved for platforms that genuinely influence customer purchases.

cards.headline: CISA developed cybersecurity incident response plan during active breach
cards.teaser: The federal cybersecurity agency had to create its incident playbook while responding to a security breach involving exposed passwords.
cards.body:
In May, cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that a security researcher at GitGuardian discovered exposed passwords in a publicly accessible GitHub repository. A CISA contractor employee had uploaded the sensitive credentials to the public repository.

The incident forced CISA to develop its incident response playbook while simultaneously managing the breach. The situation exposed gaps in the agency's preparedness protocols, requiring staff to create response procedures as containment efforts were underway.

cards.headline: Researchers use quantum error correction to continuously adjust processor performance
cards.teaser: A new technique applies reinforcement learning to recalibrate quantum computing systems using error data.
cards.body:
Scientists have developed a method to constantly recalibrate quantum processors using error correction information. The approach employs reinforcement learning algorithms that analyze error patterns to make ongoing adjustments to control systems.

Quantum computers are highly sensitive to environmental interference and internal errors that can disrupt calculations. The new technique uses data from quantum error correction processes to feed back into the control algorithms, allowing the system to adapt its operations in real time rather than relying on static calibration settings.

cards.headline: Plant-eating dinosaur species discovered in Thailand
cards.teaser: The newly identified dinosaur, named Uragasaurus kalasinensis, measured as long as a cricket pitch and lived 150 million years ago.
cards.body:
Paleontologists have identified a new herbivorous dinosaur species in Thailand called Uragasaurus kalasinensis. The animal was roughly the length of a cricket pitch, making it a substantial plant-eater of its time.

The dinosaur lived approximately 150 million years ago during the Late Jurassic period.

cards.headline: Police use increased drone surveillance to enforce fireworks laws
cards.teaser: Expanded aerial monitoring during Independence Day resulted in a $100,000 fine for illegal fireworks violations.
cards.body:
Law enforcement and fire departments deployed additional drones to monitor illegal fireworks activity around Independence Day, leading to a $100,000 penalty for violations. The enhanced surveillance effort represents a growing trend of using unmanned aerial systems for code enforcement.

Drones provide authorities with aerial views that can identify fireworks launches across wider geographic areas than ground patrols. The technology allows officials to document violations and track sources of illegal fireworks displays more effectively than traditional enforcement methods.

hero.headline: Will Jordan becomes New Zealand's all-time leading try scorer with hat-trick against Italy
hero.body:
New Zealand winger Will Jordan set a new national record by becoming the All Blacks' all-time leading try scorer during a 47-17 victory over Italy in the Nations Championship. The 26-year-old scored three tries in the match, reaching 50 international tries in just 56 Test appearances.

Jordan's hat-trick performance was the standout feature of New Zealand's dominant display. His 50th try, which came during the match, surpassed the previous record and established him as the country's most prolific try scorer in international rugby history.

The Canterbury Crusaders player has demonstrated remarkable consistency since making his Test debut. His record of scoring at such a high rate across relatively few appearances places him among the most efficient finishers in international rugby. His speed, positioning, and finishing ability have made him a key attacking weapon for the All Blacks throughout his career.

New Zealand's comprehensive victory highlighted the gulf in quality between the two sides. The 30-point winning margin reflected the All Blacks' superiority, with Jordan's clinical finishing exemplifying their attacking prowess. Italy mounted some resistance but were unable to contain New Zealand's offensive threats throughout the encounter.

The achievement adds to New Zealand's rich rugby heritage. Jordan joins a distinguished list of All Blacks players who have made significant contributions to international rugby, though his pace in reaching this milestone sets him apart from predecessors. He accomplished the feat in fewer appearances than other record holders managed.

With potentially several years remaining in his international career, Jordan has the opportunity to extend his record considerably beyond 50 tries. This could make the mark increasingly difficult for future All Blacks players to surpass, further cementing his legacy in New Zealand rugby.

The Nations Championship victory extends New Zealand's recent form in the competition. The result demonstrates the team's continued strength and their ability to perform convincingly against opposition at all levels. Jordan's performance exemplifies the attacking depth available to the All Blacks and their capacity to dominate matches through clinical finishing.

The record represents a significant personal achievement for Jordan, marking him as one of the most prolific try scorers in Test rugby history at his stage of career development. His consistency in finding the try line has been a hallmark of his international appearances, establishing him as a cornerstone of New Zealand's attacking strategy moving forward.

cards.headline: France defeats Australia in Brisbane with six-try performance
cards.teaser: Aaron Grandidier Nkanang scored twice on debut as France rallied to beat the Wallabies, extending Australia's losing streak to six matches.
cards.body:
France fought back to defeat Australia in Brisbane with a commanding six-try performance. Debutant Aaron Grandidier Nkanang was among the try scorers, crossing twice on his first appearance for the French side.

The victory extended Australia's losing streak to six consecutive defeats under coach Joe Schmidt. The Wallabies struggled to contain France's attacking threat in what proved a costly display at home.

cards.headline: Cammy Devlin joins Rangers from Hearts on free transfer
cards.teaser: Midfielder Cammy Devlin signed with Rangers under freedom of contract after departing Hearts.
cards.body:
Rangers have signed midfielder Cammy Devlin after he departed Hearts at the end of his contract. The move was completed on a free transfer, with Devlin expressing his delight at joining the Glasgow club. He described the opportunity as "an absolute honour and privilege."

Devlin's arrival strengthens Rangers' midfield ahead of the new season, bringing experience from his time in Scottish football with Hearts.

cards.headline: Two Czech players to contest Wimbledon women's final
cards.teaser: Karolina Muchova and Linda Noskova will face each other in an all-Czech Wimbledon final.
cards.body:
Wimbledon will crown a Czech champion after Karolina Muchova and Linda Noskova both advanced to the women's singles final. The matchup marks a significant achievement for Czech tennis, which has consistently produced top-level players in recent years.

Former player Naomi Broady attributed the Czech success to the nation's strong development system and coaching infrastructure. The all-Czech final highlights the depth of talent emerging from the country's tennis programs, which have helped multiple players reach the upper levels of the sport.

cards.headline: England captain Harry Kane describes golf outing with President Trump
cards.teaser: Harry Kane revealed he once played golf with United States President Donald Trump, calling the experience surreal.
cards.body:
England captain Harry Kane has revealed that he once played golf with US President Donald Trump. Kane described the experience as "surreal" when discussing the encounter during media appearances ahead of England's World Cup quarter-final against Norway.

The striker did not elaborate on specific details about the golf outing, such as when or where it took place. Kane's comments came as England prepared for their upcoming matches in the tournament.

cards.headline: Jude Bellingham returns to key role for England at World Cup
cards.teaser: Jude Bellingham has regained his central importance to England during the World Cup tournament.
cards.body:
Jude Bellingham has staged a remarkable resurgence with England at the World Cup, reclaiming his position as an indispensable midfielder for the team. Senior football correspondent Sami Mokbel has documented the 21-year-old's return to prominence during the tournament, highlighting how his performances have become central to England's approach.

The midfielder's combination of technical ability and physical presence has proven crucial in the latter stages of the competition, marking a significant turnaround in his influence within the squad.

cards.headline: Jordan Pickford sets England goalkeeping record at World Cup
cards.teaser: England goalkeeper Jordan Pickford entered the World Cup history books with a new record.
cards.body:
Jordan Pickford established a new milestone for England goalkeepers during World Cup competition. Chief football writer Phil McNulty questioned whether the Everton keeper has received adequate recognition for his achievements with the national team.

Pickford has been England's first-choice goalkeeper for several years, providing consistency between the posts. His World Cup record adds to a body of work that includes crucial saves in major tournaments, though debate continues about how his performances are evaluated compared to other top goalkeepers.

hero.headline: Randolph Mantooth, Star of NBC's Emergency!, Dies at 80
hero.body:
Randolph Mantooth, the actor who portrayed firefighter-paramedic Johnny Gage on the NBC television series Emergency!, died at age 80. The show, which aired from 1972 to 1979, followed Los Angeles County Fire Department paramedics and helped popularize emergency medical services across the United States.

Mantooth played John Gage alongside Kevin Tighe, who portrayed Roy DeSoto, in the series produced by Jack Webb. The show depicted the daily lives and rescues of Station 51's paramedics, combining action sequences with medical drama. Emergency! is credited with raising public awareness of paramedic services and inspiring many viewers to pursue careers in emergency medicine.

Born in Sacramento, California, Mantooth became synonymous with the role that defined much of his career. The character of Johnny Gage became a cultural touchstone during the 1970s, representing the then-emerging profession of paramedics in American healthcare. The series ran for six seasons and spawned several television movies that continued into the late 1970s.

After Emergency! concluded, Mantooth continued working in television and theater, though he remained most closely associated with his paramedic role. He frequently appeared at events celebrating first responders and emergency medical professionals. The actor's portrayal helped legitimize the paramedic profession during a period when emergency medical services were expanding nationwide.

Mantooth's death marks the loss of a figure who shaped how Americans understood emergency medical care through popular culture. His work on Emergency! contributed to broader acceptance and support for paramedic programs that became standard across the country in the decades following the show's debut.

cards.headline: Jay-Z Performs Reasonable Doubt 30th Anniversary Show at Yankee Stadium
cards.teaser: The rapper brought out multiple guests including Beyoncé, Blue Ivy Carter, Nas, and Alicia Keys for the concert celebrating his 1996 debut album.
cards.body:
Jay-Z celebrated 30 years of his landmark debut album Reasonable Doubt with a special concert at Yankee Stadium. Released in June 1996, the album marked the beginning of his legendary career, and the artist had long planned this anniversary show as a tribute to the project.

The Yankee Stadium performance brought together an impressive lineup of collaborators and artists connected to Jay-Z throughout his career. Beyoncé, Blue Ivy Carter, Nas, and Alicia Keys were among the notable performers who appeared at the event.

cards.headline: Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce Make First Public Appearance After Wedding
cards.teaser: The newlyweds attended JuJu Smith-Schuster's wedding, appearing together publicly for the first time since their own marriage.
cards.body:
Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce appeared at the wedding of JuJu Smith-Schuster, marking their first public outing as a married couple. Photographs showed the pair holding hands at the event.

The appearance follows their recent wedding, which had not been previously documented in public settings. Smith-Schuster is a former teammate of Kelce, who plays for the Kansas City Chiefs. The couple attended the ceremony together, with sources describing their appearance as glamorous.

cards.headline: Oregon Withdraws Motion to Delay Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger
cards.teaser: The Oregon attorney general's office dropped its request to postpone the $111 billion media merger, which could now close as soon as July 22.
cards.body:
The Oregon attorney general's office withdrew its motion to delay the closing of the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, according to a filing submitted in Multnomah County Circuit Court in Portland. The $111 billion deal could now close as early as July 22.

Several states, including Oregon and California, are investigating the merger. Despite the ongoing investigations, Oregon has removed its legal barrier to the transaction's completion. The withdrawal was filed on Friday, clearing one obstacle to the media companies' combination.

cards.headline: Constable's The Hay Wain Displayed in Suffolk for First Time
cards.teaser: The painting, which depicts a Suffolk scene, has been brought to the county where it was set for the first time in its history.
cards.body:
The Hay Wain, John Constable's painting of a Suffolk landscape, arrived in Suffolk for the first time. The work, one of the most recognized paintings in British art, has never previously been displayed in the county it portrays.

The painting shows a rural scene from Suffolk, featuring a hay wain (a type of horse-drawn cart) in a river landscape. Despite its Suffolk subject matter, the artwork had remained outside the county since its creation until now.

cards.headline: Colombia Expands Production Capacity as Bogotá Audiovisual Market Concludes
cards.teaser: The 17th edition of BAM saw increased attendance with 2,336 accredited participants and 271 industry activities as Colombia adds a massive soundstage.
cards.body:
Colombia's Bogotá Audiovisual Market concluded its 17th edition on July 10, drawing 2,336 accredited participants. The event hosted 271 industry activities and facilitated 882 one-on-one business meetings between projects and international partners.

The market highlighted Colombia's strengthening role in global audiovisual production. The series Rookies, which features a Narcos star, earned recognition among the event's honored projects. Colombia also expanded its production infrastructure with a new massive soundstage.

cards.headline: Nick Aldis Announces Tag Team Match for WWE Saturday Night's Main Event
cards.teaser: The reinstated SmackDown general manager revealed CM Punk and Cody Rhodes will team up for the upcoming event, before Gunther attacked him.
cards.body:
Nick Aldis announced that CM Punk and Cody Rhodes will team together in a tag match at WWE Saturday Night's Main Event. The SmackDown general manager, who was recently reinstated to his position, made the announcement during a WWE broadcast.

Following the announcement, Gunther attacked Aldis. The incident occurred after the show went off the air, with exclusive footage captured by WWE cameras showing the altercation. Aldis had been reinstated as general manager prior to making the match announcement.

hero.headline: Trump fires two Democratic election commissioners ahead of midterms
hero.body:
President Trump has dismantled the U.S. Election Assistance Commission by removing all remaining members of the independent federal agency devoted to election administration, drawing accusations that he is attempting to manipulate the upcoming midterm elections.

Trump fired the two Democratic commissioners, Thomas Hicks and Benjamin Hovland, by email on Thursday, effective immediately. The sole remaining Republican commissioner, Christy McCormick, was pushed to resign rather than fired outright. A fourth seat had already been vacant since Republican Donald Palmer departed for the Heritage Foundation earlier this year. With no commissioners remaining, the agency cannot vote to take any formal action.

The White House justified the removals by citing the president's authority to remove officials and referenced a recent Supreme Court ruling that expanded his power to fire heads of independent agencies. However, election law scholars say the ruling's application to bipartisan bodies like the EAC remains untested, since Congress deliberately structured the commission around an equal partisan split.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the dismissals a "brazen attempt" to seize control of elections. "Firing every remaining member of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission months before the midterms is a brazen attempt to seize control of our elections before a single vote is cast," Schumer wrote on social media. He noted that the agency certifies voting systems and helps election officials run secure elections.

Derrick Johnson, president of the NAACP, accused Trump of rigging the election because he fears voters will reject his policies. "Donald Trump knows that in November voters will reject everything he stands for," Johnson said, pledging that the organization would work to send people to the polls.

The Election Assistance Commission distributes federal election security grants, maintains the national mail voter registration form, certifies voting machines against federal standards, and advises state and local officials. Created following the disputed 2000 election, it does not run elections itself but serves as a resource for cash-strapped states.

With the commission paralyzed, it cannot update voting standards or the federal registration form. This potentially freezes changes the administration has pushed for, including a citizenship documentation requirement that courts have already partially blocked.

Benjamin Hovland, one of the fired commissioners, warned that losing the agency risked administrative mistakes during the midterms. Democratic secretaries of state criticized the firings as irresponsible. Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar said the EAC plays a critical role supporting state and local election officials, and the dismissals would make it harder for election administrators to do their work.

Replacements would require Senate confirmation, a process that could extend well past the midterm elections.

cards.headline: US demands Iran confirm Strait of Hormuz open after strikes resume
cards.teaser: The United States is demanding Iran affirm that the Strait of Hormuz remains open to shipping as the two countries continue exchanging strikes in the strategic oil chokepoint.
cards.body:
The U.S. is demanding that Iran commit to allowing free passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stop firing on ships, as tensions escalate between the two nations. Vice President JD Vance and other U.S. officials are expected to participate in negotiations scheduled for Saturday in Oman.

Recent strikes have already deterred shipping through the critical waterway. Data shows a significant decline in the number of vessels—many carrying oil and gas—using the route following attacks this week. The Strait of Hormuz is essential for global energy supplies, making access to the passage a key concern for international markets.

cards.headline: ICE shooting of Texas man sparks calls for investigation
cards.teaser: The fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by federal immigration officers in Texas has prompted calls for an independent investigation into what officials acknowledge was mistaken identity.
cards.body:
Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national, was shot and killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent during a traffic stop in Houston. Officials have acknowledged the shooting was a case of mistaken identity. Salgado Araujo was driving a van with construction crew members when the incident occurred.

Three men who were in the vehicle are disputing the Trump administration's account of events, denying that Salgado Araujo weaponized his vehicle against agents. According to their lawyer, the witnesses are facing pressure to sign deportation orders. Advocates are calling for the Department of Homeland Security to release bodycam footage, though DHS states the agents involved were not wearing cameras.

cards.headline: Minnesota governor pulls National Guard early from Washington
cards.teaser: Minnesota Governor Tim Walz is withdrawing his state's National Guard troops from Washington early as pressure mounts on Democratic governors to end deployments.
cards.body:
Minnesota Governor Tim Walz is withdrawing his state's National Guard from Washington, D.C. ahead of schedule. The decision reflects growing opposition among Democratic governors to maintaining troop deployments in the capital during President Trump's administration.

Walz's move adds pressure on other Democratic governors, particularly Michigan's, to reconsider their own National Guard presence in Washington. The deployment has become a flashpoint in disputes between state leaders and the federal government over how state military resources are used.

cards.headline: Intelligence reports suggest Iran plans to target Trump
cards.teaser: Israel has shared intelligence with the United States indicating Iran intends to assassinate President Trump as the ceasefire between the two nations deteriorates.
cards.body:
Intelligence shared by Israel with the U.S. indicates Iran is planning to assassinate President Trump, according to reports this week. The reported threat highlights tensions between Washington and Tehran as a ceasefire between the two countries has broken down.

Vice President JD Vance and other U.S. officials are expected to participate in negotiations resuming Saturday in Oman, where discussions will include Iran's activities in the Strait of Hormuz.

cards.headline: Questions surround Trump-endorsed Freedom Fuel gas stations
cards.teaser: President Trump has promoted 25 Freedom Fuel gas stations in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, but little public information exists about the stations or their operators.
cards.body:
President Trump has recently promoted 25 "Freedom Fuel" gas stations operating in Pennsylvania and New Jersey. These stations are offering fuel at relatively low prices.

Trump's endorsement of the stations aligns with his broader push for gas retailers to reduce their prices. However, the ownership structure and operational details of the Freedom Fuel locations remain largely undisclosed to the public.

cards.headline: Apple files lawsuit against OpenAI over alleged information theft
cards.teaser: Apple has sued OpenAI, claiming the artificial intelligence company attempted to steal confidential information through job interviews with Apple employees.
cards.body:
Apple is suing OpenAI, alleging the AI company stole trade secrets to develop hardware devices. According to the lawsuit, OpenAI recruited Apple employees and persuaded them to share confidential materials, product designs, and other proprietary information. The suit claims senior leadership at OpenAI, including a longtime former employee, directed the misconduct.

The legal action marks a significant rupture between the two companies, which have previously worked as industry partners. The lawsuit was filed in California federal court.
